idiom_name: private_constant key class plus private_class_method :new (runtime call rules, all bypassable)
implementation_notes: Ruby's visibility keywords are runtime call rules: private and protected set method visibility, private_class_method :new stops ordinary construction, and Module#private_constant makes an outside reference to the constant raise NameError - but every one of them can be stepped over, because send invokes private methods, allocate builds an instance without new, const_get and module_eval read private constants, and instance_variable_get reads state. The closest structure is therefore to hold the key class in a private constant inside the owning module and expose exactly one narrow public method, accepting that the rest is convention held by review and linters rather than by the language. If the boundary has to hold, it must be a real boundary: a process, a service or a native extension.
code_sketch:
module Pool
  class Key                       # held in a private constant, not a public one
    private_class_method :new
  end

  def self.restricted(_key) = :ok
end

# Pool::Key.new                    -> NoMethodError at run time
# Pool.const_get(:Key).send(:new)  -> works: the 'grant' is not a boundary
pitfalls: send ignores visibility, allocate skips initialise, and const_get/module_eval reach private constants - each defeats the token without a warning.
private_constant only guards the module namespace; instance_variable_get and Method#unbind reach everything else.
All of Ruby's checks happen while the program runs, so a mistake shows up in production rather than in a build.
alternative: No compile-time equivalent exists, so hold the key in a private constant inside its module (private_constant) and expose exactly one narrow entry point, treating private_class_method :new and #private as call-site discipline only - send, allocate, const_get and module_eval all step over them. Enforce the boundary with linters and review, and when it must actually hold, move the implementation behind a process, a service or a native extension: Ruby cannot fail the program before it runs.
